A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RLoT work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–L are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v2 reports original RLoT benchmark results, cross-model and cross-task transfer experiments, computational measurements, and component analyses in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds training, state-noise, PRM-correlation, prompt-sensitivity, and failure-case results.

M1.justification: The default five-block navigator, Double-Dueling-DQN training, PRM rewards, and inference pipeline are retained. However, new Appendix F.2 describes binary self-evaluation states, while Section 3.2 retains 1–3 scoring and Listing 1 additionally permits 0. The PDFs do not resolve whether state encoding actually changed or the new description is inaccurate. The Double-DQN experiment is presented as an alternative-training analysis.

E1.justification: The mathematics, STEM, and commonsense task coverage remains. Appendix F.2 adds evaluation scenarios with randomized states and 30% or 50% corruption of navigator state inputs, extending the tested input conditions. The added MATH-500 column remains within the existing mathematical-reasoning coverage rather than establishing a new task domain.

E2.justification: v3 Table 10 adds evaluated Least-to-Most and SelfCheck baselines to the comparison in v2 Table 9. Litesearch also joins the efficiency comparison in v3 Table 11, although it already appeared in v2's accuracy comparison. Appendix A.2 adds a Double-DQN training comparison. The existing main benchmark comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: v3 substantially expands the supplementary evaluation design: Appendix A.2 tests 5,000-episode training and Double-DQN; F.2 introduces state-corruption controls; H.2 measures intermediate PRM-score correlations with final correctness; and K.3 tests rephrased action prompts. Table 10 adds MATH-500 evaluation. These are added protocols; the default 3,000-episode training and existing main experimental settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine convergence beyond 3,000 episodes and optimizer choice, failure from inaccurate states versus inappropriate actions, sensitivity to state corruption, cross-domain PRM calibration, and action-prompt wording. These substantially extend validation of the navigator's operation and reliability. The logic-block removal ablation is retained and moved from v2 Table 17 to v3 Table 6, rather than newly conducted.

E5.justification: v2 Table 9 presents performance point estimates; v3 Table 10 explicitly reports means and standard deviations across five repeated runs throughout the extended baseline comparison. This newly documents performance uncertainty without establishing an increase from a previously specified performance-run count. The separate three-repeat latency uncertainty reporting is retained in v3 Table 8.

E6.justification: Main Table 2 scores are unchanged, but the appendix results expand substantially. v3 Table 10 reports new five-run summaries, MATH-500 scores, and additional baselines; for example, RLoT GPQA is 44.78 ± 0.71 versus the earlier point entry of 44.64, not an established method improvement. New training, noise, correlation, latency, prompt-variation, and failure outcomes are reported. v3 Tables 16–17 also correct averages while retaining task scores, including RLoT's 73.34 to 72.18 correction.

T1.justification: The likelihood expression, formal MDP preliminaries, and discounted-return definition are retained. No new theorem, proof, or formal derivation is introduced. The added PRM correlations and mathematical failure examples are empirical analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction qualify superiority as occurring 'in most cases,' with the maximum improvement associated with challenging situations. This modestly narrows the performance claim. The central contributions—adaptive logic structures, the lightweight navigator, transferability, and comparison with much larger LLMs—remain unchanged, as does the 13.4% headline.

C2.justification: Appendix B now explains two concrete failure mechanisms: erroneous self-evaluation can misdirect the navigator, and unnecessary refinement can corrupt correct reasoning. New discussion interprets noise tests as evidence of state-dependent decisions, PRM correlations as explaining cross-domain transfer, and prompt rephrasing as supporting reliance on adaptive structures. This substantially expands the earlier reliability and transferability discussion, although the new correlations do not themselves establish the claimed causal mechanism.

D1.justification: v3 supplies exact rephrased action templates in Listings 11–17, specifies four candidates for SelfCheck, and adds instance counts to the existing reasoning-pattern table. The abstract changes the advertised code location from an anonymous mirror to a named GitHub repository, while the reproducibility statement and Appendix J retain the anonymous reference. Existing implementation settings and pipeline details are largely unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds Least-to-Most prompting by Zhou et al. (2023) and SelfCheck by Miao et al. (2024), positioning them among fixed reasoning workflows. The main related-work discussion and positioning against predefined structures, search methods, and LLM fine-tuning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 gathers training discussion into a dedicated Section 4.2, reorganizes the ablation discussion, and adds descriptive subsections within several appendices. It also makes limited abstract and introduction edits and changes the publication header. Most existing prose and the overall narrative remain intact; the added scientific material does not amount to extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The evidence displays are substantially expanded and reorganized. Existing learning curves are redistributed between the main text and Appendix A; new figures show longer training and failure cases. New tables display state noise, PRM correlations, and prompt sensitivity, while extended baseline tables gain dataset, uncertainty, and timing information. The unchanged logic-block ablation moves into the main text. The original framework diagram and logic-block plots are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens an already broadly evaluated paper through five-run uncertainty reporting, corrected averages, targeted robustness analyses, and explicit failure explanations. These improve scrutiny of the results and clarify operational limitations without changing the main benchmark findings. The gains are limited by the conflicting binary-versus-graded state descriptions and interpretations that attribute more explanatory force to PRM correlations than those measurements establish. Overall, the added validation supports a modest net improvement.
